Product Architecture Framework

OrderxPay

Mobile-first order invoicing & payment platform for Ghanaian retailers — merchant app, back office, user flows, and wireframe reference.
Merchant App Back Office Ghana PSP / BoG Act 987 WhatsApp Commerce Prepared July 30, 2026

Section 01

Executive Summary

OrderxPay is a mobile-first order-to-cash tool for Ghanaian retailers who already sell over the phone, WhatsApp, and SMS but have no structured way to invoice or collect payment. The product does not attempt to replace how these merchants sell — it formalises the last mile: turning a verbal or chat order into an itemised invoice with an instant, no-login payment link, and giving the merchant a single source of truth for what was ordered, what was paid, and what is still owed.

Because OrderxPay is not itself a licensed payment institution, every collection and payout rail in this framework is designed around a third-party Payment Service Provider (PSP) — Ghana's Payment Systems and Services Act, 2019 (Act 987) makes this a legal requirement, not a design preference. This document treats that regulatory boundary as a first-class architectural constraint, not an afterthought bolted on at the end.

This framework covers four things in depth:

  • A full module breakdown of the OrderxPay merchant app and the Back Office platform, including modules the original brief did not mention but that are necessary to run this at scale (Sections 4, 7 and 8).
  • Two end-to-end user flows — a phone/chat-initiated sale, and a customer-initiated order from a shared catalog page (Section 12).
  • A companion set of high-fidelity, mobile-first wireframes for the merchant app and desktop wireframes for the Back Office, delivered as separate interactive HTML files (Section 13).
  • A phased delivery roadmap and the key regulatory, technical and business risks to plan around (Sections 14–15).

Section 02

Regulatory & Compliance Foundation (Ghana)

OrderxPay's architecture is downstream of four Ghanaian legal frameworks. Getting these right early avoids expensive re-architecture later — particularly around KYC tiering and settlement, which are the two areas the business plan already anticipates (minimum KYC to trade, full KYC to withdraw).

2.1 Payment licensing — Payment Systems and Services Act, 2019 (Act 987)

The Bank of Ghana (BoG) operates a tiered Payment Service Provider (PSP) licensing framework: Dedicated Electronic Money Issuer (DEMI), PSP Enhanced, PSP Medium, PSP Standard (Ghanaian-owned only), PSP Scheme, and Payment Financial Technology Service Provider (PFTSP). Operating unlicensed electronic money or payment aggregation services is an offence under the Act.

Architectural implication: OrderxPay should sit above this line entirely — it must never touch, hold, or move customer funds directly. Every collection (mobile money, card, USSD) and every payout to a merchant should be executed by a BoG-licensed PSP or bank partner via API, with OrderxPay acting purely as an orchestration and record-keeping layer.

2.2 AML / KYC — Anti-Money Laundering Act, 2020 (Act 1044)

Ghana's AML regime (enforced by the Financial Intelligence Centre) requires risk-based customer due diligence, transaction monitoring, and suspicious transaction reporting from obliged entities and their regulated partners. The Ghana Card is the primary national identity document used for biometric verification.

Tier 0 — Minimum KYC

Phone number + OTP + business name. Enough to send invoices and collect payment, but funds settle to a PSP-held balance, not a direct payout.

Tier 1 — Full KYC

Ghana Card, business registration (or sole proprietor certificate), proof of MoMo/bank account, liveness/selfie check. Required before any payout.

Ongoing monitoring: velocity and volume thresholds per merchant that trigger a review before an anomalous payout is released — e.g. a sudden 10x jump in daily collections.

2.3 Data Protection Act, 2012 (Act 843)

Any entity that collects or processes personal data in Ghana must register as a Data Controller with the Data Protection Commission (renewable every two years) before processing begins. This applies squarely to OrderxPay: merchant KYC data, customer names/phone numbers captured on invoices, and WhatsApp conversation content are all personal data.

Architectural implication: register early as a Data Controller; build consent capture into merchant onboarding (merchants collect customer data on OrderxPay's behalf, so a data processing agreement between OrderxPay and the merchant is needed too); design data retention/deletion tooling from day one.

2.4 GRA Electronic VAT Invoicing (E-VAT / VSDC)

Since October 2022, Ghana Revenue Authority (GRA) has been rolling out a real-time invoicing clearance model: VAT-registered businesses must transmit every invoice to GRA's Virtual Sales Data Controller (VSDC) for validation before it is issued, receiving a clearance number, digital signature and QR code back. As of 2026 this applies to all VAT-registered taxpayers, with offline invoices requiring transmission within 24 hours of connectivity returning.

Architectural implication: OrderxPay itself is not the taxpayer — the merchant is. But since OrderxPay generates the invoice on the merchant's behalf, it should be built to optionally integrate with a Certified Invoicing System / VSDC connector so VAT-registered merchants can stay compliant. Treat this as a roadmap item (Section 14) rather than an MVP blocker, since most small retail merchants sit under Ghana's simplified/Modified Taxation Scheme.

2.5 USSD numbering — National Communications Authority (NCA)

USSD short codes are regulated as Special Numbering Resources by the NCA. In practice, businesses go through a USSD aggregator / CPaaS partner that already holds cross-network connections, rather than negotiating with MTN, Telecel and AirtelTigo individually.

Regulatory summary for the pitch deck / investor conversation
  • OrderxPay is a technology and orchestration layer, not a payment institution — it never custodies funds.
  • Tiered KYC (minimum-to-trade, full-to-withdraw) mirrors what BoG/AML already expects, not just good UX.
  • Data Controller registration with the Data Protection Commission should happen before public launch.
  • E-VAT / GRA invoicing compliance is a merchant-facing add-on, not a blocker for MVP.

Section 03

System Architecture Overview

OrderxPay is best modelled as four layers: customer-facing surfaces (no app, no login), the merchant app, a shared core platform of backend services, and a third-party integration layer that does everything requiring a license OrderxPay does not hold. The Back Office platform sits alongside the merchant app, consuming the same core services with an internal, permissioned view.

3.1 Layer summary

  • Customer-facing surfaces — the payment link (hosted checkout), the hosted catalog/item-list page, and the USSD session. None require an account or app install.
  • OrderxPay Merchant App — the mobile-first app merchants use to onboard, manage items, create and send invoices, chat with customers, and review records.
  • WhatsApp Business integration — technically a channel, but significant enough to treat as its own module (Section 6), since it's the primary channel per the brief.
  • Core Platform Services — shared backend services used by both the merchant app and the Back Office: identity/KYC, the order/invoice engine, the fee & commission engine, notifications, ledger & reconciliation, risk screening, audit logging, and reporting.
  • Back Office Platform — the internal admin application for merchant lifecycle management, settlement oversight, integrations configuration, pricing control, and business reporting.
  • Third-party integration layer — licensed PSPs for mobile money/card/USSD collection and payout, a WhatsApp Business Solution Provider (BSP), SMS/email providers, and (optionally) a GRA-certified invoicing connector.

Section 04

OrderxPay Merchant App — Module Breakdown

This expands the nine features in the original brief into buildable modules, and adds the modules a production system needs around them.

4.1 Onboarding & Tiered Identity

  • Self-serve sign-up: phone number + OTP (via SMS provider) + business name + business category.
  • Tier 0 (minimum KYC): enough to create items and send/collect invoices; funds accrue to a PSP-held balance.
  • Tier 1 (full KYC): Ghana Card capture + selfie liveness check, business registration or sole-proprietor certificate upload, bank/MoMo payout account — required before the first payout request.
  • KYC status indicator on the merchant home screen with a clear "Verify to withdraw" call to action.
  • Progressive-disclosure design: never block order-taking or collection behind full KYC — only block payout.

4.2 Catalog & Item Management

  • Preset item library: name, unit price, quantity/unit type, category, optional image upload (camera or gallery), availability toggle (In stock / Out of stock / Made to order).
  • Quick-add: create a one-off custom item inline while building an order, without polluting the saved catalog.
  • Bulk actions: duplicate item, bulk price update, archive vs. delete.
  • This same catalog powers the hosted catalog page customers browse (Section 4.6) — single source of truth, no duplicate data entry.

4.3 Order & Invoice Engine

  • Build an order from the catalog (tap to add, quantity stepper) or a quick custom line item.
  • Auto-calculates subtotal, service charge (per the merchant's fee-allocation setting, Section 4.8), and grand total.
  • Generates a shareable invoice: unique reference number, itemised breakdown, and a payment link / QR.
  • Invoice lifecycle states: Draft → Sent → Viewed → Partially Paid → Paid → Expired / Cancelled → Refunded.
  • Re-issue / amend an invoice (e.g. after a customer-requested order is confirmed) while preserving the audit trail of the original request.

4.4 Messaging & Distribution

  • Send the invoice/payment link via SMS, WhatsApp, email, or "copy link" for any other channel.
  • Delivery status per channel (sent / delivered / read where the channel supports it, e.g. WhatsApp).
  • Template library for common messages (order confirmation, payment reminder, thank-you receipt) the merchant can tweak.

4.5 Payment Collection

  • Hosted checkout page (mobile-optimised HTML): Mobile Money (MTN MoMo, Telecel Cash, AirtelTigo Money) and card, via the PSP's SDK/redirect.
  • Optional USSD payment path: a USSD session tied to the merchant's account and the specific invoice reference, for feature-phone customers or low-data situations.
  • Partial payment support (deposit now, balance later) with the ledger tracking amount paid vs. amount owed.
  • Idempotent webhook handling from the PSP so a retried callback never double-credits an invoice.

4.6 Customer-Initiated Ordering (Catalog Flow)

  • Hosted, mobile-optimised catalog page generated from the merchant's saved item list — shareable as a WhatsApp broadcast link, status update, or SMS.
  • Customers browse, select items and quantities, and submit an order request — this is a request, not a payable invoice.
  • Requests land in the merchant app as a pending queue; the merchant confirms availability (per line item), adjusts quantities, or declines, then the engine auto-generates the payable invoice from the confirmed request.

4.7 Records, Ledger & Reporting (merchant-facing)

  • Searchable, filterable records sheet: customer, date/time, items, amount invoiced, amount paid, outstanding balance, status, channel used.
  • Per-transaction detail view / digital receipt, shareable back to the customer.
  • Simple merchant analytics: best-selling items, daily/weekly collections, average order value, repeat customers.
  • CSV/PDF export for the merchant's own bookkeeping or accountant.

4.8 Fees & Settlement Configuration

  • Service charge allocation: Customer Only (default), Merchant Only, or Split — with a percentage-allocation input for the split option, shown transparently on the invoice before payment.
  • Payout/settlement preferences (bank account or MoMo wallet), payout schedule (on-demand vs. scheduled), and minimum payout threshold.
  • OrderxPay's platform rate is a single blended figure — built from the PSP's collection fee (~1.5–2.5%), the PSP's payout fee (~1%), and OrderxPay's own margin — so merchants see one number, not a fee stack, when they check how the 3–5% commission is calculated.

Collection and payout fees are not symmetric, and the product deliberately doesn't treat them as if they were. The collection fee is known and attributable the instant a specific customer pays a specific invoice. The payout fee is charged per withdrawal batch — a merchant might settle thirty orders in one payout — so at the moment any single customer is checking out, there is no way to know what share of that eventual batch fee belongs to their order. Only one of the two fees is genuinely meterable per transaction.

  • The merchant-facing Service Charge settings screen (not the customer-facing checkout) shows the full breakdown on request — collection fee, payout fee, and OrderxPay's margin — so merchants understand what the blended rate covers, without the checkout screen getting more complicated.
  • Payout fee handling defaults to merchant-absorbed, deducted at settlement (Section 7.2). A merchant who wants customers, or a Customer/Merchant split, to help cover it does so by raising their blended rate, not by adding a second live fee line at checkout — same economic effect, without asking a customer to fund an estimate of a cost that hasn't happened yet.
  • The customer-facing checkout page (Section 5.1) is unaffected by any of this: it always shows a single "Service charge" line, however the merchant's blended rate was built underneath it.

4.9 Multi-User / Staff Roles — recommended addition

Many retailers operate with a shop assistant or family member handling sales. A Staff role (can create/send invoices, cannot change payout settings or view full KYC/bank details) prevents the founder from becoming a bottleneck as merchants grow, and is a natural upsell/retention feature later.

4.10 Notifications

  • Push/SMS/WhatsApp alerts to the merchant for: payment received, order request pending, payout processed, KYC status change.
  • Customer-side confirmations: payment received receipt, order status updates.

4.11 Delivery Coordination — recommended addition

OrderxPay does not operate delivery itself — the same non-custodial posture that governs payments (Section 2.1) applies here: OrderxPay orchestrates and surfaces options, a licensed or independent third party executes. Delivery is offered through a tiered model that a merchant can mix and match, configurable per order rather than fixed platform-wide.

  • Tier 1 — Merchant's own delivery contact: a name and phone number (and optionally a flat fee per zone) attached to the merchant profile. Zero integration cost, always available, and formalises what most merchants already coordinate over WhatsApp today.
  • Tier 2 — Deep-link directory to verified third-party delivery apps: OrderxPay stores the merchant's business location once and captures the customer's delivery address at the point delivery is chosen, then generates a pre-filled deep link (pickup, drop-off, and product pre-selected) into whichever provider the merchant has opted into. The customer taps through, sees the provider's own live pricing, and books there — OrderxPay is never a party to that transaction.
  • Tier 3 — API-level aggregator integration (future roadmap, not committed): a business delivery API (in the style of Uber Direct) that returns real-time status and tracking to the merchant, rather than a one-way deep link. Meaningfully more engineering and a commercial negotiation with a provider — worth doing once delivery volume justifies it, not before.
  • Per-order configurability: the merchant decides, order by order, whether to quote delivery at invoice creation (bundled into the total the customer pays through OrderxPay) or leave delivery for the customer to arrange separately after payment. Fee handling follows the same logic — bundled into the OrderxPay invoice or fully external — and can differ by delivery method, since a merchant's own rider has a fee OrderxPay can know in advance while a third-party app's live price it cannot.
  • The Back Office maintains the list of verified delivery providers (Section 7.3) rather than hardcoding it into the app, since deep-link parameters and product availability change on the provider's schedule, not OrderxPay's.

Section 05

Customer Payment Experience

Since there is deliberately no customer-facing app, the checkout and catalog pages carry the entire burden of trust and usability. They need to load fast on 3G, work on low-end Android devices, and never require an account.

5.1 Hosted checkout page

  • Single-purpose, lightweight HTML page (not a full SPA) — itemised invoice, merchant name/logo, total, and payment method tabs.
  • Mobile Money and card via the PSP's hosted fields or redirect (keeps OrderxPay out of PCI-DSS scope entirely — cardholder data never touches OrderxPay's own servers).
  • Clear, real-time status after payment: success, pending (common with MoMo approval delays), or failed with a retry path.

5.2 USSD fallback

For feature phones or zero-data situations: customer dials a shortcode tied to the merchant, enters the invoice reference (or it is pre-filled if dialled from an SMS deep-link), and approves with their mobile money PIN — no internet needed at any point.

5.3 Designing for no login

The invoice reference number in the link/QR is the only "credential" — treat it as a bearer token: single-use where possible, short expiry window, and rate-limited to prevent guessing.

Section 06

WhatsApp Integration Module

WhatsApp carries both the conversational commerce layer and a meaningful share of collection volume in the Ghanaian market, so it deserves its own module rather than being treated as "just another channel."

6.1 Business Solution Provider (BSP)

Direct use of Meta's Cloud API is possible, but most SME-facing products in West Africa go through a BSP (e.g. Twilio, 360dialog, Gupshup, or Ghana-based providers such as Hubtel or Arkesel) for template approval support, number provisioning, and local billing. Evaluate on: local billing in GHS, template-approval turnaround, uptime SLA, and whether they support the catalog/commerce API in addition to plain messaging.

6.2 Catalog sync

The merchant's OrderxPay item catalog can sync to a WhatsApp Business catalog, so customers see the same items, prices and availability natively inside WhatsApp, not just via the hosted web link.

6.3 Auto-response builder

  • Merchant-configurable greeting message, away message, and quick-reply templates (e.g. "Do you have this in stock?", "Send me your price list").
  • A generator that drafts sample auto-response scripts the merchant can edit in plain language — this is the feature explicitly requested in the brief.
  • Template messages (outside the 24-hour customer-service window) must go through Meta/BSP approval — the builder should flag this distinction so merchants understand why some messages need pre-approval and others don't.

6.4 Compliance guardrails

  • Opt-in capture before marketing-style broadcasts (WhatsApp commerce policy + Ghana's Data Protection Act both require a real consent trail, not just an assumption).
  • Clear separation in the data model between transactional messages (order/payment updates) and marketing messages, since they are billed and governed differently.

Section 07

Back Office Platform — Module Breakdown

7.1 Merchant Lifecycle Management

  • Merchant list with KYC tier, status (Pending / Active / Restricted / Suspended), GMV, and join date.
  • KYC review queue: view submitted Ghana Card / business registration documents, approve or reject with a reason, request additional documents.
  • Merchant detail view: profile, catalog snapshot, transaction history, payout history, notes/flags from support or compliance staff.
  • Ability to suspend a merchant (e.g. on suspicious activity) which immediately blocks new invoice creation and payouts, without deleting historical data.

7.2 Collections, Settlement & Payout Ledger

  • Real-time reconciliation view: gross collections in, PSP fees, OrderxPay commission, net amount payable to each merchant.
  • Payout batch management: scheduled batch runs plus manual/ad-hoc payout trigger for support cases, each producing an auditable payout record.
  • Exception queue for failed payouts, PSP webhook mismatches, or disputed transactions.

7.3 System Integrations Hub

  • Configuration screens (with securely stored credentials, never displayed in plaintext after entry) for: Payment Gateway/PSP, WhatsApp BSP, SMS/Email provider, USSD aggregator, and the optional GRA E-VAT connector.
  • Per-integration health status, webhook delivery logs, and the ability to rotate keys or swap providers without a code deployment.
  • A maintained list of verified delivery providers and their deep-link parameters (Section 4.11 / 9.4), editable without a release — provider apps change their URL schemes and product availability on their own schedule.

7.4 Pricing, Commission & Feature Configuration

  • Global default commission rate (e.g. 3–5%) with the ability to set merchant-specific overrides.
  • Default service-charge allocation setting and whether merchants may override it.
  • Feature flags for rolling out new modules (e.g. USSD payments, WhatsApp catalog sync) to a subset of merchants first.
  • Because the platform rate is a blended figure (collection + payout + margin, Section 4.8), pricing configuration here tunes the payout-fee and collection-fee components and the margin as separate inputs, not one combined percentage — so a change in a PSP's payout pricing doesn't require manually re-deriving the new blended number.

7.5 Revenue & Commission Dashboard / Reporting

  • Commission revenue over time, gross merchandise value (GMV) processed, active vs. dormant merchants, blended take-rate.
  • Cost tracking against revenue: PSP fees, WhatsApp BSP/message costs, SMS costs — so net margin per transaction is visible, not just top-line commission.
  • Exportable reports for finance/accounting and investor reporting.

7.6 Risk & Fraud Monitoring — recommended addition

Velocity rules (sudden spike in volume or value), duplicate-device/duplicate-Ghana-Card detection across merchant accounts, and a manual review queue feeding the AML/KYC obligations in Section 2.2.

7.7 Dispute & Refund Management — recommended addition

A structured way to log a customer dispute against an invoice (e.g. paid but goods not received), track its resolution, and trigger a refund through the PSP where warranted.

7.8 Admin Users, Roles & Permissions — recommended addition

Role-based access for the back-office team itself: Super Admin, Compliance/KYC Reviewer, Finance/Settlement, Support — each scoped to only the data and actions they need.

7.9 Audit Trail & Compliance Logging — recommended addition

Immutable log of every sensitive back-office action (KYC approval/rejection, manual payout, fee override, merchant suspension) with who, what, and when.

7.10 Support / Helpdesk Console — recommended addition

A place for support staff to look up a merchant's or customer's transaction, resend a payment link, or escalate a payout issue, without needing raw database access.

Section 08

Additional Recommendations Not Covered in the Original Brief

Beyond the module-level additions above, these are cross-cutting product and architecture decisions worth deciding early rather than retrofitting.

AreaRecommendationWhy it matters
Offline / low-connectivity designMerchant app should queue actions (item creation, invoice send) locally and sync when connectivity returns; catalog/checkout pages should be lightweight for 3G.Ghana's retail merchants often work in areas with inconsistent connectivity; a fragile app loses trust fast.
Idempotency & webhook safetyEvery PSP webhook and USSD callback must be idempotent and signature-verified.Prevents duplicate payment credits and protects against spoofed callbacks.
PCI scope avoidanceNever handle raw card data on OrderxPay servers — always PSP-hosted fields/redirect.Keeps compliance burden and liability with the licensed PSP, not OrderxPay.
Merchant risk tieringNew merchants start with lower daily transaction/payout limits that increase with track record and KYC tier.Standard fraud-mitigation pattern; mirrors how PSPs already treat OrderxPay itself.
Data retention & deletionBuild a data lifecycle policy and a deletion workflow.Required in substance by the Data Protection Act; also reduces breach impact.
LocalizationEnglish first; design copy and WhatsApp templates so Twi/Ga phrasing can be added without re-architecture.Broadens reach beyond English-first urban retailers.
Merchant credit-readinessStructure the transaction ledger so it can later feed a lending/BNPL risk model.A clean, verified sales history is the biggest asset a merchant-payments platform can build toward future working-capital products.
White-label potentialKeep merchant-facing branding (catalog, checkout, receipts) themeable per merchant from day one.Cheap to build early, expensive to retrofit; improves each merchant's own brand trust.
Backup & disaster recoveryAutomated backups of ledger/order data with a tested restore process; documented RPO/RTO.Financial transaction records cannot be the place a startup discovers it skipped this.
Product analyticsFunnel analytics (sign-up → first invoice → first payment) separate from the financial ledger.Needed to see where merchant activation is stalling, independent of finance reporting.

Section 11

Non-Functional Requirements

Performance

Hosted checkout/catalog pages should target sub-2-second load on 3G — plain HTML/CSS with minimal JS, image compression on merchant photos, CDN delivery.

Security

No card data storage (PSP-hosted fields only); encrypted at-rest KYC documents; signed, idempotent webhooks; role-based Back Office access.

Availability

Payment collection and invoice viewing need the highest uptime target — a merchant unable to send an invoice loses a sale in real time.

Scalability

Order/invoice engine and ledger as stateless services behind a queue, scaling independently of e.g. the WhatsApp auto-response builder.

Compliance-by-design: KYC tiering, consent capture, and audit logging (Sections 2, 6.4, 7.9) should be core services every module calls into, not features bolted onto individual screens.

Section 12

User Flows

12.1 Flow A — Phone Call / Chat-Initiated Order & Payment

The standard case: a customer already knows what they want and reaches the merchant directly.

  1. Customer calls or messages the merchant (phone call, WhatsApp, SMS) describing what they want to buy.
  2. Merchant opens OrderxPay, selects the relevant preset items (or adds a one-off custom item) and sets quantities.
  3. The app calculates the subtotal, applies the merchant's service-charge allocation rule, and shows the total.
  4. Merchant sends the invoice — with its embedded payment link — via whichever channel the customer prefers.
  5. Customer opens the link on their phone; no account or login is required. They see an itemised breakdown and total due.
  6. Customer pays via Mobile Money, card, or by dialling the USSD code tied to the merchant's account.
  7. The PSP confirms the transaction via webhook; OrderxPay updates the invoice status in real time (handling partial payments if only a deposit is made).
  8. Both merchant and customer receive an instant confirmation notification.
  9. The completed order and payment are written to the merchant's records sheet with status "Paid" (or "Partially Paid").

12.2 Flow B — Customer-Initiated Order from the Catalog Page

The self-serve case: a customer browses what's available and initiates the request themselves.

  1. Merchant shares the hosted catalog link — via WhatsApp broadcast, WhatsApp status, or SMS — showing preset items with photos, prices and availability.
  2. Customer opens the link and browses the catalog on their phone.
  3. Customer selects items and quantities and taps "Request Order" — this is a request, not yet a payable invoice, per the requirement that nothing is payable until the merchant confirms.
  4. The request appears in the merchant's app as a pending order request.
  5. Merchant reviews the request against real stock/availability, confirms as-is, adjusts quantities/items, or declines with a reason.
  6. On confirmation, the engine auto-generates the payable invoice directly from the confirmed request — the merchant doesn't have to rebuild it from scratch.
  7. The invoice and payment link are sent back to the customer via WhatsApp, SMS, or email.
  8. Customer pays via Mobile Money, card, or USSD on the hosted checkout page.
  9. PSP confirms payment; both parties are notified instantly.
  10. The order and payment are logged on the records sheet, and item availability/stock is updated if the merchant tracks it.

12.3 Optional delivery step (either flow)

Both flows above can include an optional delivery step, configured per order rather than fixed platform-wide (Section 4.11). If the merchant offers delivery at invoice creation, a delivery option and address are attached before the invoice is sent, and the fee is bundled or external depending on the method chosen. If delivery is left for after payment, the merchant and customer coordinate it separately — through the merchant's own contact or a deep link into a verified provider — once the order is already paid and recorded.

Section 13

Wireframe Reference & Screen Inventory

High-fidelity, mobile-first wireframes for the merchant app and desktop wireframes for the Back Office are delivered as two separate interactive HTML files alongside this document, so they can be viewed full-size and navigated screen to screen. This section is the index of what each file contains.

OrderxPay App — screens

Onboarding & minimum KYC · Home/dashboard · Item creation · Create & send invoice · Customer payment page · Incoming order request confirmation · Transaction & order records · WhatsApp catalog & auto-response settings · Full KYC upgrade & payout · Service charge settings.

Back Office — screens

Admin shell/navigation · Revenue & operations dashboard · Merchant management + KYC review · Collections & payout ledger · System integrations hub · Pricing & global settings · Reports · Admin users & roles · Audit log.

Section 14

Recommended Phased Delivery Roadmap

A pragmatic MVP-first sequencing — get the core loop (item → invoice → payment → record) live and trusted before layering on WhatsApp automation and Back Office sophistication.

PhaseDurationScope
Phase 0 — FoundationsWeeks 1–3PSP partner selection & integration contract, Data Protection Commission registration, core data model, Tier 0/Tier 1 KYC design.
Phase 1 — MVP core loopWeeks 4–10Merchant onboarding, catalog/item management, order & invoice engine, hosted checkout (MoMo + card), SMS/link sharing, basic records sheet, minimal Back Office (merchant list, manual payout), delivery Tier 1 (merchant's own delivery contact on invoices).
Phase 2 — Distribution & self-serve orderingWeeks 11–16WhatsApp send/receive integration, hosted catalog page, customer-initiated order requests, service-charge allocation options, full KYC & payout automation, delivery Tier 2 (deep-link directory to verified providers, per-order fee handling).
Phase 3 — WhatsApp automation & Back Office depthWeeks 17–22Auto-response builder, WhatsApp catalog sync, integrations hub, pricing/commission configuration, revenue dashboard & reporting.
Phase 4 — Trust, risk & scaleWeeks 23–28USSD payment path, risk/fraud monitoring, dispute & refund management, audit log, admin roles & permissions, staff/multi-user roles.
Phase 5 — Hardening & growthWeeks 29–34Offline-first refinements, GRA E-VAT connector (opt-in), localization groundwork, merchant analytics, white-label theming.

Delivery Tier 3 (API-level aggregator integration, Section 4.11) is deliberately not placed on this roadmap — it is a future direction to revisit once delivery volume justifies the engineering and commercial negotiation, not a Year 1 commitment.

Section 15

Key Risks & Mitigations

RiskMitigation
Regulatory exposure if OrderxPay is perceived to be operating as an unlicensed payment institution.Contractually and architecturally keep all fund custody with the licensed PSP partner; publish this clearly in terms; register as a Data Controller early.
PSP outage or MoMo network downtime blocks all collections.Design for a secondary PSP/rail where commercially feasible; clear customer messaging and retry paths during known MoMo incidents.
WhatsApp template rejection or account suspension by Meta disrupts the primary channel.Keep SMS as an always-available fallback channel; follow WhatsApp commerce policy strictly on opt-in and template categorisation.
Merchant KYC fraud (fake Ghana Card, stolen identity) enabling money laundering through invoices.Ghana Card biometric verification, velocity/anomaly monitoring (7.6), staged payout limits tied to KYC tier and track record.
Low-end devices / poor connectivity causing app abandonment during onboarding or checkout.Lightweight checkout/catalog pages, offline queuing in the merchant app, USSD fallback for hardest-to-reach customers.
Fee-allocation model (customer/merchant/split) causing customer confusion or trust issues at checkout.Always show the fee breakdown transparently on the payment page before the customer pays, regardless of who is charged.
